identity.what_it_is: A small historic harbour beach in Fremantle, Western Australia, with a written history dating to European settlement; site of a former whaling station and precinct traditionally known to the Whadjuk Noongar people as Manjaree.
identity.where: Fremantle, Western Australia; the shore below the Round House, just south of Arthur Head, at the entrance to Fremantle Harbour (South Mole starts at its northern side). Coordinates 32.0585°S, 115.7418°E.
identity.warnings: The 1930s-40s alias 'City Beach' is also the name of an unrelated, better-known Perth suburb/beach — do not conflate in later copy. Bundle otherwise supports slug/name match with no near-dupe risk.

spike_candidates.statement: A tunnel dug by Round House prisoners in 1837-38 linked the beach to High Street in just five months; cliff-cutting after 1880 has since shrunk it from 57m to 45m.
spike_candidates.tension: A tourist-friendly harbourside amenity was built by convict labor under a private whaling investor, and its shrinking length is a physical record of erasure rather than preservation.

spike_candidates.statement: On 4 September 1829 the ship Marquis of Anglesea wrecked on Bathers Beach in a gale, giving its name to Anglesea Point — a landmark now buried under reclaimed land.
spike_candidates.tension: The point named to memorialize the wreck no longer physically exists; it was land-filled out of visibility.

spike_candidates.statement: The Fremantle Whaling Company built its station at Bathers Beach in 1837 but the market collapsed by 1840, and by 1850 its operator, Daniel Scott, had pivoted from whaling to housing convicts.
spike_candidates.tension: The beach's founding commercial industry failed within a few years, and its promoter's next business was profiting from the colony's convict system the same year whaling here ended.

facts.fact: Bathers Beach is also known as Whalers Beach and is a section of Fremantle coastline with a written history dating to European settlement.
facts.quote: bathers beach, also known as whalers beach, is a section of coastline that has a written history since the european settlement of what is now called fremantle, western australia.

facts.fact: In the 1890s the beach was bounded to the south by the long and short jetties.
facts.quote: in the 1890s it was bounded to the south by the long and short jetties.

facts.fact: In the 1930s and 1940s the beach was called City Beach.
facts.quote: in the 1930s and 1940s it was called city beach.

facts.fact: The water offshore from the beach has also been called Bathers Bay.
facts.quote: the water offshore has also been called bathers bay.

facts.fact: The beach lies below the Round House, just south of Arthur Head, at the entrance to Fremantle Harbour, with the South Mole starting at its northern side.
facts.quote: it is the shore below the round house and is located just south of arthur head, at the entrance to fremantle harbour with the south mole starting at its northern side.

facts.fact: The Bathers Beach precinct is traditionally known as Manjaree by the Whadjuk Noongar people and served as an important meeting and trading site.
facts.quote: the bathers beach precinct is traditionally known as manjaree by the whadjuk noongar people, serving as an important meeting place and trading site.

facts.fact: On 4 September 1829 the ship Marquis of Anglesea dragged its anchors and wrecked on Bathers Beach during a gale.
facts.quote: on 4 september 1829 marquis of anglesea dragged her anchors and was wrecked on bathers beach during a gale.

facts.fact: The rocky promontory that defined the beach's southern end, now hidden beneath reclaimed land, was named Anglesea Point after the wreck, and the Fremantle Long Jetty extended from it.
facts.quote: a rocky promontory, which defined the southern end of the beach (now hidden beneath reclaimed land) and from which the fremantle long jetty extended, was subsequently named anglesea point.

facts.fact: Daniel Scott, Fremantle's harbour master, a businessman and town council chair, made a substantial investment in the Fremantle Whaling Company in 1837.
facts.quote: daniel scott, who was the local harbour master, businessman and chair of the town council, made substantial investment in the fremantle whaling company in 1837.

facts.fact: The whaling company built a 57-metre-long (187 ft) tunnel linking the beach to High Street to move heavy equipment and products.
facts.quote: an impressive investment was made when the company created a 57-metre-long (187 ft) tunnel that linked the beach to high street, allowing easy access for transporting heavy equipment and products.

facts.fact: The tunnel was dug in five months and completed in January 1838.
facts.quote: it was dug in five months and completed in january 1838.

facts.fact: The tunnel's rapid construction was possible because prisoners from the Round House were used as labor, the rock was easily pick-axed, and the work was overseen by Henry Willey Reveley.
facts.quote: this rapid progress was possible because prisoners from the round house were used, the rock was capable of being mined with a pick axe, and the work was overseen by henry willey reveley.

facts.fact: The tunnel is today only 45 metres (148 ft) long because the cliffs were cut back sometime after 1880.
facts.quote: today the tunnel is only 45 metres (148 ft) long as the cliffs were cut back some time after 1880.

facts.fact: Two local whaling companies started in 1836, and the Fremantle Whaling Company was based at Bathers Beach.
facts.quote: there were two local whaling companies started in 1836, but the fremantle whaling company was based here.

facts.fact: The whaling company, which included Liverpool investors, had mixed fortunes and the market collapsed in 1840.
facts.quote: this company, which included investors in liverpool, had mixed fortunes as the market collapsed in 1840.

facts.fact: Despite the market collapse, the company did build a whaling station at Bathers Beach.
facts.quote: however the company did build a whaling station at bathers beach.

facts.fact: The whaling station included the tunnel plus a number of buildings and a jetty where whales were processed.
facts.quote: the station included the tunnel and a number of buildings and a jetty where whales could be processed.

facts.fact: Daniel Scott rented the whaling station in the 1840s and operated whaling ships including Napoleon and Merope.
facts.quote: scott rented this station in the 1840s and he also operated a number of whaling ships including napoleon and merope.

facts.fact: The whaling business was not driven hard, and Scott sold his whaling boats and equipment in 1850.
facts.quote: the whaling business does not appear to have been driven hard and scott sold up his whaling boats and equipment in 1850.

facts.fact: The Fremantle Whaling Company ceased operating in 1850.
facts.quote: the fremantle whaling company also ceased to operate that year.

facts.fact: In 1850, the same year whaling ended, Scott's new task was accommodating convicts.
facts.quote: (scott's new task was accommodating convicts that year.)

facts.fact: The range of activities at the beach since the 1820s, including whaling, has attracted archaeological interest.
facts.quote: due to the range of activities since the 1820s, including whaling, the area adjacent to the beach has attracted archaeological interest.

facts.fact: Nuala Randall's 1987 paper 'Western Australia's Shore Based Whaling Heritage' covers the area's whaling history in the Bulletin of the Australian Institute for Maritime Archaeology.
facts.quote: randall, nuala (1987), "western australia's shore based whaling heritage", bulletin of the australian institute for maritime archaeology, 11 (2): 33- 36

facts.fact: Jack McIlroy's 1986 paper 'Bathers Bay Whaling Station, Fremantle, Western Australia' was published in Australian Historical Archaeology.
facts.quote: mcilroy, jack (1986). "bathers bay whaling station, fremantle, western australia" (pdf). australian historical archaeology. 4.

facts.fact: Martin Gibbs's 2010 book 'The Shore Whalers of Western Australia: Historical Archaeology of a Maritime Frontier' (Sydney University Press) covers the site.
facts.quote: gibbs, martin (2010). the shore whalers of western australia: historical archaeology of a maritime frontier. university of sydney, n.s.w.: sydney university press. pp. 15, 22, 42, 127. isbn 978-1920899622.

facts.fact: A 1990 Heritage Council of Western Australia report, 'Arthur Head Stage Three,' documents excavation and conservation of a 19th-century retaining wall at Bathers Beach.
facts.quote: mcilroy, jack; fremantle (w.a.: municipality). council; heritage council of western australia; campbell, rob mck; andrews, bill (1990), arthur head stage three: the excavation and conservation of a 19th century retaining wall at bathers beach, fremantle, western australia
facts.source_title: Bathers Beach, Fremantle - Wikipedia (citing McIlroy et al. 1990)
